title: What did Carney term ‘outrageous’ this week? Take our business and investing news quiz
html:
Prime Minister Mark Carney boards a plane in Ottawa, on Wednesday.Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press

Welcome to The Globe and Mail’s business and investing news quiz. Join us each week to test your knowledge of the stories making headlines. Our business reporters come up with the questions, and you can show us what you know.

This week: Barrick Mining of Toronto filed paperwork for its initial public offering of a minority share in its North American business, shares of GFL Environmental tumbled and the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board is laying off dozens of employees. Take our quiz and find out what happened in business.

c. Mr. Carney lambasted auto maker Stellantis, calling its move to sell its car plant in Brampton, Ont., to defence contractor Roshel “completely outrageous.” The Prime Minister vowed to protect workers and ensure that previous government subsidies to Stellantis are returned. “Stellantis is failing to respect their commitment to the workers of this plant and also to the Canadian government and Canadians,” Mr. Carney told reporters in Montreal.

b. Such agents are commonly known as honeytraps. In the case of Nvidia, China has denied that it used a honeytrap to spy on Mr. Huang, calling such claims “groundless speculation and slander.” Rather than being a perpetrator of such deceptions, Beijing claims it is typically the victim. The Ministry of State Security, China’s top intelligence agency, regularly warns of honeytrap operations run by foreign countries for the purpose of collecting sensitive information from Chinese citizens.

a. Ms. Karniol-Tambour has been named as the first chief executive of Ottawa’s new Canada Strong Fund. The sovereign wealth fund will have an initial capital commitment of $25-billion and aims to invest in nation-building projects and companies deemed strategic. Ms. Karniol-Tambour is currently the co-chief investment officer at U.S.-based hedge fund manager Bridgewater Associates.

c. Spain’s embattled government confronted a nationwide strike this week after union leaders called for a public protest over soaring housing costs and stagnant wages. The general strike, the nation’s first since 2012, came ahead of a snap election on Nov. 29 called by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

b. The cable companies say that Sportsnet shouldn’t be allowed to charge customers an extra $13 per month to get NHL games on Monday nights. Eastlink, Cogeco and SaskTel filed a complaint with the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission alleging that Rogers Communications acted in an anti-competitive manner by introducing the surcharge this season.

d. Peter Munk, the founder of Barrick, was a vocal Canadian patriot. His successors appear to be following a different path. The company announced this week that it will be listing the shares for its new unit, to be called American Barrick Gold Corp., in New York. The miner said earlier in the year it intended to seek a secondary stock listing for American Barrick in Toronto, but that no longer appears to be part of the plan.

a. CoreWeave rents out AI supercomputers and builds AI-focused data centres. Its shares jumped after the New Jersey-based company reported strong revenue growth and calmed investors’ nerves by signalling a pullback from its recent borrowing binge.

d. GFL shares fell after the board of the big trash hauler said it was formally shutting down a review of unsolicited bids to take the company private for more than US$20-billion. Known for its bright green garbage trucks, GFL was founded in Vaughan, Ont., in 2007 by entrepreneur Patrick Dovigi. It is now headquartered in Miami.

c. You think you have problems picking winning stocks? So does CPPIB. It is laying off dozens of employees from its active equities division, which invests in public companies and those that are soon to be listed publicly. Somehow, in the middle of a great stock market boom, the division has managed to lose $6-billion over five years. Ouch.

a. Whatever happened to elbows up? Nutrien is preparing to spend between US$500-million and US$1-billion to build an export terminal at the Port of Longview, Wash. The company considered Canadian ports but selected the Washington option as its preferred site in November last year. This week it presented a development plan to the port’s board of commissioners.

d. Anthropic plans to set aside up to 20 per cent of the shares offered in its IPO for retail investors in select markets, a larger allocation than is typical for major U.S. offerings where shares have historically gone primarily to institutional investors and wealthy clients.

b. Investors who bought SpaceX shares on the day that the company began trading on June 12 are nursing losses of around 19 per cent compared to a gain of 2.5 per cent in the broad S&P 500 index over the same period. Investors who managed to snag shares in the company’s highly anticipated IPO are doing considerably better, but are still far from making a fortune. They are sitting on gains of about 3.5 per cent.
summary: Test your recollection of the top stories of the week ending Nov. 13
